topics.name: Diodes
topics.kicker: One-way valves for electric current · Turn AC into DC
topics.dates: First vacuum-tube version by John Ambrose Fleming, 1904
topics.briefing: A diode is an electronic part that lets electric current flow in only one direction, like a one-way valve for electricity. Most diodes today are made by joining two kinds of silicon, called p-type and n-type, and they are used to turn the alternating current from a wall outlet into the direct current that electronics need. Light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, are diodes that glow when current passes through them.
topics.answerHtml: diodes (accept diode; prompt on rectifiers or p-n junctions; do not accept “LEDs” or “transistors”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1904, John Ambrose Fleming built an early version of these devices from a vacuum tube, calling it an “oscillation valve,” to detect radio signals for Guglielmo Marconi’s wireless company. Modern versions of these devices are usually made from silicon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic components that let electric current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: Lee de Forest added a third electrode, a wire grid, to the vacuum-tube type of these devices, creating the Audion, which could amplify signals. Early crystal radio sets used a crude type of these devices called a “cat’s whisker,” a thin wire touching a crystal of galena.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these two-terminal parts that act as one-way valves for electric current.

tossups.p: In 1874, Karl Ferdinand Braun [“BROWN”] found that a metal point touching certain crystals could rectify electricity, the first semiconductor example of these devices. Modern examples of these devices are made at a junction between p-type and n-type silicon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic components that let current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: Zener [“ZEE-ner”] types of these devices, named for Clarence Zener, are designed to conduct backward once a set breakdown voltage is reached, so they can hold a voltage steady. When an ordinary one of these devices is reverse biased, it blocks nearly all flow.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components, made from p-n junctions, that pass current in just one direction.

tossups.p: Leo Esaki [“eh-SAH-kee”] shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics after inventing a “tunnel” type of these devices, in which the current drops as the voltage rises over a certain range. Ordinary types of these devices are called “non-ohmic,” since their current does not grow in proportion to the voltage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic parts, used as rectifiers, that let current flow only one way.

tossups.p: Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano, and Shuji Nakamura won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics for making efficient blue light-emitting versions of these devices, which made bright, energy-saving white lighting possible. In 1962, Nick Holonyak Jr. made the first practical light-emitting one that gave off visible red light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic components that let current pass in only one direction.

tossups.p: Four of these devices arranged in a diamond-shaped bridge make a full-wave rectifier, which flips the backward half of each cycle of alternating current so that both halves come out flowing the same way. A single one of these devices instead blocks every backward half-cycle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components that change AC into DC by letting current flow in just one direction.

tossups.p: Schottky [“SHOT-kee”] types of these devices join a metal directly to a semiconductor, which lets them switch on with less voltage than usual. On a circuit diagram, one of these devices is drawn as a triangle pointing at a short bar.
tossups.r: A painted stripe marks its cathode end. For 10 points, name these components that let current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: A silicon one of these devices needs about 0.7 volts across it in the forward direction before it conducts well. That happens when its p side is connected to the positive side of a battery, a setup called forward bias.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components, used as rectifiers, that block current flowing the wrong way.

tossups.p: At the heart of most of these devices is a thin depletion region, where electrons from the n-type side have filled the “holes” on the p-type side. That region acts as a barrier that only a large enough forward voltage can push current across.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic parts, used in rectifiers, that let current flow just one way.

tossups.p: A solar cell is basically a large, flat version of these devices: light striking its p-n junction knocks electrons loose and drives them around a circuit. Light-emitting versions of these devices do the reverse, giving off light when electrons cross the junction and fill holes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components, which pass current in only one direction and can turn AC into DC.

tossups.p: Blu-ray players read discs using a laser type of these devices that gives off blue-violet light, while CD players use a type that gives off infrared light. Other types of these devices glow in many colors in traffic lights and screens.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic components that let current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: Varactor [“vuh-RAK-ter”] types of these devices behave like capacitors whose value changes with the voltage across them, so they can tune radios without moving parts. Placing an ordinary one of these devices in line with a battery holder protects a gadget if the batteries go in backward.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components, often marked with a stripe, that let current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: In the early 1880s, Thomas Edison noticed that a heated filament inside a light bulb sent electricity across the vacuum to a nearby metal plate, but only when the plate was connected to the positive side. That “Edison effect” is the basis of vacuum-tube types of these devices.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components that let electric current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: A TV remote control flashes coded pulses of infrared light from a light-emitting type of these devices, and the TV picks them up with a light-sensitive type of these devices. Both types are built around a junction of p-type and n-type material.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components that let current flow in only one direction, often used as rectifiers.

trap.title: The device, not LEDs
trap.body: Light-emitting diodes (LEDs) are just one kind of this device, so this page does not accept “LED” or “light-emitting diode” when a tossup is about the general one-way part. Players also confuse it with the transistor, which usually has three terminals and can amplify or switch signals, and with the triode, the three-electrode vacuum tube that Lee de Forest made by adding a grid. Saying “rectifier” earns only a prompt, since that word names the job, not the part.
trap.fix: One-way flow, AC to DC, p-n junctions, anode and cathode, Fleming’s valve, and Zener types mean diodes. Three terminals, amplifying, and switching mean transistors. If a question asks specifically for the devices that give off light, then answer “LEDs.”
trap.line: Real answer line: diodes (accept diode; prompt on rectifiers or p-n junctions; do not accept “LEDs” or “transistors”)

topics.name: Ampère’s law
topics.kicker: Magnetic fields from electric currents · One of Maxwell’s equations
topics.dates: Named for André-Marie Ampère; corrected by Maxwell in the early 1860s
topics.briefing: Ampère’s law says that if you add up the magnetic field all the way around any closed loop, you get a number set by the electric current passing through that loop. Physicists use it to find the magnetic field around a straight wire or inside a coil without hard calculations. James Clerk Maxwell later added a missing piece, and the corrected law became one of the four Maxwell’s equations that describe electricity, magnetism, and light.
topics.answerHtml: Ampère’s law (accept Ampère’s circuital law or Ampère–Maxwell law; prompt on Ampère or Maxwell’s equations; do not accept “Biot–Savart law” or “Faraday’s law”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This law gives the wrong answer in the gap of a charging capacitor unless it includes a “displacement current” term, which James Clerk Maxwell added in the early 1860s. With that term, a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, just as a current does.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating the magnetic field around a closed loop to the electric current passing through the loop.

tossups.p: Using this law with a circular path around a long, straight wire shows that the wire’s magnetic field falls off as one over the distance from the wire. This law plays the same role for magnetism that Gauss’s law plays for electricity, making problems with lots of symmetry easy.
tossups.r: It is applied by drawing an imaginary closed loop around a current. For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations.

tossups.p: Inside a doughnut-shaped coil called a toroid, this law shows that the magnetic field weakens with distance from the doughnut’s center, while outside the coil the field is zero. This law also gives the nearly uniform field inside a long, straight coil called a solenoid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, that links a magnetic field to the electric current that makes it.

tossups.p: Outside a coaxial cable whose inner wire and outer sleeve carry equal currents in opposite directions, this law predicts no magnetic field at all, since no net current passes through a loop drawn around the cable. When using this law, only the current that passes through the chosen closed path counts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating the magnetic field around any closed loop to the current through it.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell called this law’s namesake “the Newton of electricity.” That namesake began his experiments in 1820, within weeks of learning that Hans Christian Ørsted had made a compass needle swing using a current.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, named for a French physicist, about the magnetic field produced by electric currents.

tossups.p: The original form of this law works only for steady currents that do not change over time. Maxwell’s corrected version of this law, together with Faraday’s law of induction, predicted waves of electric and magnetic fields traveling at the speed of light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, which says that electric currents produce magnetic fields that circle around them.

tossups.p: The Biot–Savart [“bee-OH suh-VAR”] law gives the same answers as this law, but this law is far easier to use when a problem has a lot of symmetry. The constant in this law, mu-naught, is called the permeability of free space.
tossups.r: This law says that the magnetic field added up around a closed loop is proportional to the current through it. For 10 points, name this law.

tossups.p: This law contains the constant mu-naught, the permeability of free space, which is about four pi times ten to the negative seventh in SI units. That constant multiplies the current that passes through the closed path in this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that links the magnetic field around a loop to the current through it, one of Maxwell’s four equations.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake called his new field of study “electrodynamics.” When using this law around a wire, a right-hand rule gives the direction of the magnetic field: point your thumb along the current, and your fingers curl the way the field circles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, about the magnetic fields made by currents.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake also showed in 1820 that two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other, a result described by a separate “force law” named for him. James Clerk Maxwell later added a displacement current term to this law.
tossups.r: This law relates the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current inside it. For 10 points, name this law.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake, one of 72 scientists whose names are engraved on the Eiffel Tower, was largely self-taught and became a professor at the École Polytechnique [“ay-KOHL po-lee-tek-NEEK”] in Paris. Maxwell’s corrected version of this law is one of his four famous equations.
tossups.r: This law relates the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current passing through it. For 10 points, name this law.

tossups.p: This law shows that the magnetic field just outside a long, tightly wound solenoid is nearly zero, while inside it equals mu-naught times the number of turns per meter times the current. It works easily around a straight wire, where the field is equally strong all the way around a circle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, that links a magnetic field to the current that makes it.

tossups.p: Faraday’s law says that a changing magnetic field makes an electric field, while the corrected form of this law says that a changing electric field makes a magnetic field. That pairing led James Clerk Maxwell to predict that light is an electromagnetic wave.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current through the loop.

tossups.p: Applying this law inside a thick wire with current spread evenly across it shows that the magnetic field grows in proportion to the distance from the wire’s center, then weakens outside the wire. The magnetic field lines around the wire form closed circles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, that relates a magnetic field to the electric current producing it.

tossups.p: The left side of this law adds up the magnetic field all the way around a closed path, a quantity called the field’s circulation. This law’s namesake proposed that tiny loops of current inside magnets cause their magnetism.
tossups.r: The right side of this law is mu-naught times the current through the path. For 10 points, name this law.

trap.title: Which electromagnetism law?
trap.body: Several laws of electricity and magnetism show up together. This law links the magnetic field circling a closed loop to the current passing through it; Gauss’s law links the electric field through a closed surface to the charge inside; Faraday’s law says a changing magnetic field makes a voltage; and the Biot–Savart law builds up a magnetic field piece by piece. The same French physicist also has a separate force law about parallel wires, and the unit of current carries his name, so saying just “Ampère” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Closed loops (Amperian loops), the current enclosed, solenoids, toroids, and Maxwell’s displacement current mean this law. Closed surfaces and enclosed charge mean Gauss’s law; induction, generators, and Lenz’s law mean Faraday’s law; adding up the field from tiny pieces of wire means the Biot–Savart law.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ampère’s law (accept Ampère’s circuital law or Ampère–Maxwell law; prompt on Ampère or Maxwell’s equations; do not accept “Biot–Savart law” or “Faraday’s law”)

topics.name: Spin (physics)
topics.kicker: A particle’s built-in angular momentum · Up or down for electrons
topics.briefing: Spin is a built-in amount of angular momentum that electrons, protons, and many other particles carry, as if they were tiny spinning tops, though nothing is actually turning. An electron’s spin can point only “up” or “down,” and spin makes electrons and protons act like tiny magnets: lined-up electron spins make permanent magnets, and MRI scanners flip the spins of hydrogen nuclei. Particles with half-integer spin (like 1/2 or 3/2) are called fermions, and those with whole-number spin are called bosons.
topics.answerHtml: spin (accept spin angular momentum, intrinsic angular momentum, or spin quantum number; prompt on angular momentum)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ralph Kronig thought of this property early in 1925 but did not publish it after Wolfgang Pauli criticized the idea. Later that year, George Uhlenbeck [“OO-len-bek”] and Samuel Goudsmit [“GOWD-smit”] proposed it to explain why some spectral lines split into close pairs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum of particles, which for an electron can point only up or down.

tossups.p: Hendrik Lorentz objected that if this property came from an electron actually turning, the electron’s surface would have to move faster than light. In 1928, Paul Dirac’s equation for the electron produced this property automatically.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum property, a built-in angular momentum that equals one-half for electrons.

tossups.p: In 1922, Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach [“GAIR-lahk”] fired silver atoms through an uneven magnetic field and saw the beam split into two parts, a result later explained by this property of each atom’s outermost electron. For an electron, this property can take only two values.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum of particles, often described as “up” or “down.”

tossups.p: Wolfgang Pauli proved in 1940 that this property decides whether a particle obeys his exclusion principle. Particles with half-integer values of this property, such as electrons, are called fermions, while those with whole-number values, such as photons, are called bosons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum carried by particles such as electrons and protons.

tossups.p: A particle with a value of one-half for this property must be rotated a full 720 degrees, not just 360, before its wavefunction returns to exactly its original value. Electrons have that value of this property, which makes each electron act like a tiny magnet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum property, a particle’s built-in angular momentum, which is up or down for an electron.

tossups.p: Albert Fert and Peter Grünberg [“GROON-bairk”] won the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering giant magnetoresistance, which depends on this property of electrons and let hard drives store far more data. In iron magnets, this property of many unpaired electrons lines up in small regions called domains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum of particles, which for an electron is one-half.

tossups.p: Chemists identify molecules with NMR spectroscopy, which detects atomic nuclei that have this property. MRI scanners line up this property of hydrogen nuclei in the body with a powerful magnet, then flip it with pulses of radio waves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum of particles such as protons and electrons.

tossups.p: Hydrogen atoms in space give off radio waves 21 centimeters long when the electron flips this property to point the opposite way from the proton’s. Astronomers use that 21-centimeter line to map the spiral arms of the Milky Way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum property, a built-in angular momentum that makes particles act like tiny magnets.

tossups.p: Atoms of helium-4 have a total of zero for this property, so they act as bosons, which lets liquid helium-4 flow without any friction as a superfluid at very low temperatures. Atoms of helium-3 have a total of one-half and act as fermions instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, a particle’s built-in angular momentum, that is up or down for an electron.

tossups.p: This property explained the “anomalous” Zeeman effect, in which spectral lines split into unexpected patterns in a magnetic field. It is described by the fourth quantum number, which is either plus one-half or minus one-half.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, a particle’s built-in angular momentum, which makes each electron act like a tiny magnet.

tossups.p: Before this property was named, Wolfgang Pauli described a mysterious “two-valuedness” of the electron that classical physics could not explain. The Pauli exclusion principle says that two electrons sharing an orbital must have opposite values of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum property, which can be “up” or “down” for an electron.

tossups.p: The hypothetical graviton would have a value of two for this property, and the Higgs boson is the only known elementary particle with a value of zero. Photons and gluons each have a value of one for this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, a built-in angular momentum that is one-half for electrons.

tossups.p: This property is measured in units of h-bar, which is Planck’s constant divided by two pi, and an electron carries exactly one-half of a unit. In orbital diagrams, this property is shown by drawing each electron as an arrow pointing up or down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum carried by electrons, protons, and neutrons.

tossups.p: In the Einstein–de Haas effect, magnetizing a hanging iron cylinder makes it start to rotate, because lining up its electrons’ magnetism also lines up this property, and the total angular momentum must stay the same. Particles called fermions have half-integer values of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum of particles, which is up or down for an electron.

tossups.p: Liquid oxygen clings between the poles of a strong magnet because each oxygen molecule has two unpaired electrons with matching values of this property. Hund’s rule says that electrons fill orbitals of equal energy one at a time, all with the same value of this property, before any of them pair up.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum property, a built-in angular momentum that is “up” or “down” for an electron.

trap.title: Spin or angular momentum?
trap.body: This property is a particle’s built-in angular momentum, so plain “angular momentum” earns only a prompt here, while the angular momentum page does not accept “spin.” An electron also has orbital angular momentum from moving around the nucleus, which is a different thing, and “magnetic moment” names the tiny magnet that this property creates. Stern–Gerlach and Pauli exclusion clues can also lure a wrong buzz of “electrons” when the question asks for the property.
trap.fix: Up or down, one-half, fermions and bosons, Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, the Stern–Gerlach split, MRI, and the 21-centimeter line mean spin. If the giveaway asks for “these particles,” say electrons; if it asks for the rule that two electrons in one orbital must be opposite, say the Pauli exclusion principle.

topics.name: Gustav Kirchhoff
topics.kicker: German physicist · Circuit laws and the science of spectroscopy
topics.briefing: Gustav Kirchhoff was a German physicist who worked out two simple rules for electric circuits in 1845, while he was still a student. With the chemist Robert Bunsen, he showed that every element glows with its own pattern of colored lines, and the pair used that trick to discover cesium and rubidium and to learn what the Sun is made of. He also coined the term “black body” for a perfect absorber of light.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1857, this scientist calculated that an electric signal in a wire with no resistance would travel at about the speed of light. As a student at Königsberg [“KUR-nigs-bairg”], he had studied under Franz Neumann [“NOY-mahn”], and he later taught at Breslau, Heidelberg, and Berlin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist whose namesake circuit laws are the junction rule and the loop rule.

tossups.p: This physicist coined the term “black body” for an object that absorbs all the light that falls on it. His law of thermal radiation says that, at the same temperature, a good absorber of light is also an equally good emitter of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who discovered cesium and rubidium with Robert Bunsen.

tossups.p: In 1859, this scientist explained the dark Fraunhofer [“FROWN-hoh-fer”] lines in sunlight, showing that cooler gases absorb exactly the colors they give off when heated. He showed that sunlight passed through a sodium flame made the Sun’s dark D lines even darker.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who worked with Robert Bunsen and has namesake circuit laws.

tossups.p: Max Planck succeeded this physicist as a professor of theoretical physics in Berlin and later solved his challenge to find how the glow of a black body depends on wavelength and temperature. This man had moved to Berlin in 1875 after about twenty years at Heidelberg.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist known for both spectroscopy and electric circuit laws.

tossups.p: In 1860, this scientist and a partner found a new element in mineral water from Dürkheim [“DUR-kime”] after spotting two blue lines in its spectrum, and they named it from the Latin for “sky blue.” A year later, they found a second element named from the Latin for “deep red.”
tossups.r: Those elements are cesium and rubidium. For 10 points, name this German physicist who worked with Robert Bunsen.

tossups.p: In 1845, while still a university student, this scientist published two rules that extended Georg Ohm’s work to complicated networks. One rule follows from the conservation of electric charge, and the other follows from the conservation of energy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist whose namesake laws are used to analyze electric circuits.

tossups.p: This physicist and his chemist partner passed the light from flames colored by different salts through a prism and found that each element always produces its own set of bright lines, whatever compound it is part of. They described that method of spectrum analysis in 1860.
tossups.r: That partner, Robert Bunsen, has a lab burner named for him. For 10 points, name this German physicist.

tossups.p: This physicist found that many dark lines in sunlight line up exactly with bright lines given off by hot iron vapor, showing that the Sun contains iron. He mapped the Sun’s spectrum in great detail in the early 1860s.
tossups.r: He had earlier proved that the Sun contains sodium. For 10 points, name this German physicist who pioneered spectroscopy with Robert Bunsen.

tossups.p: In 1877, this scientist and his longtime partner became the first two winners of the Royal Society’s Davy Medal. The two men had first met at the University of Breslau and later worked together for years at Heidelberg.
tossups.r: That partner was Robert Bunsen. For 10 points, name this German physicist known for laws of electric circuits.

tossups.p: This physicist was born in 1824 in Königsberg [“KUR-nigs-bairg”], a Prussian city later renamed Kaliningrad, in Russia. He spent the last part of his career teaching theoretical physics in Berlin, where he died in 1887.
tossups.r: His junction rule says the current flowing into any point in a circuit equals the current flowing out. For 10 points, name this physicist.

tossups.p: Using his law of thermal radiation, this physicist argued that the glow given off by a perfect absorber depends only on its temperature and the wavelength, not on what it is made of. Finding the exact formula for that glow became a famous challenge.
tossups.r: This physicist’s loop rule says the voltages around any closed loop in a circuit add up to zero. For 10 points, name this German physicist.

tossups.p: According to this scientist’s three laws of spectroscopy, a hot, dense object gives off a continuous rainbow of colors, while a hot, thin gas gives off only bright lines. A cooler gas in front of a hot source makes dark lines instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist whose other namesake laws describe electric circuits.

tossups.p: This physicist’s diffraction formula put Christiaan Huygens’s [“HOY-gunz”] idea, that every point on a wave front acts as a source of new wavelets, on a firm mathematical footing. He also explained why the Sun’s spectrum has dark lines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist whose junction and loop rules help solve electric circuits.

tossups.p: This physicist and his partner heated salts of lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium, and other metals in a hot, nearly colorless gas flame, recording the pattern of colored lines each one made. They found that even a tiny trace of sodium gives a bright yellow line.
tossups.r: The flame came from a burner named for his partner, Robert Bunsen. For 10 points, name this German physicist.

tossups.p: The method of spectrum analysis that this physicist developed with a partner soon led others to new elements: William Crookes found thallium in 1861 by its bright green line, and astronomers spotted the yellow line of helium in sunlight in 1868.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who discovered cesium and rubidium with Robert Bunsen.

trap.title: The physicist, not Bunsen
trap.body: Gustav Kirchhoff and the chemist Robert Bunsen worked as a team, so spectroscopy clues, the Sun’s dark lines, and the discovery of cesium and rubidium fit both men, and this page does not accept “Bunsen.” Kirchhoff’s circuit laws are also their own answer line, so if a question asks for “these laws,” say “Kirchhoff’s laws,” not just his name.
trap.fix: Circuit laws, the junction and loop rules, black bodies, and the law of thermal radiation point to Kirchhoff; the gas burner, arsenic compounds, batteries, and geysers point to Bunsen. If the question asks for “this physicist,” give the person.

topics.name: Maxwell’s demon
topics.kicker: Imaginary molecule-sorter · Seems to break the second law of thermodynamics
topics.briefing: Maxwell’s demon is a tiny imaginary being dreamed up by the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell in 1867. It guards a little door between two boxes of gas, letting fast molecules into one side and slow ones into the other, so one side heats up and the other cools down without any work being done. That would break the second law of thermodynamics, but most physicists say the catch lies in information: the demon must remember, and eventually erase, what it learns about each molecule.
topics.answerHtml: Maxwell’s demon (prompt on demon; do not accept “second law of thermodynamics”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a 1929 paper, Leo Szilard [“SIL-ard”] imagined a one-molecule “engine” based on this thought experiment, and argued that gaining information about the molecule’s position must create at least a tiny amount of entropy. His paper’s title mentions the “intervention of intelligent beings.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this imaginary creature that sorts fast and slow gas molecules between two chambers.

tossups.p: Charles Bennett argued in 1982 that this imaginary being’s real cost comes not from measuring molecules but from eventually erasing its memory of them. By Rolf Landauer’s principle, erasing each bit of information must give off a little heat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this creature that opens a tiny door to let fast molecules go one way and slow molecules the other.

tossups.p: William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, whose title names a temperature scale, gave this imaginary being its common name in an 1874 article. Its creator had described it as a being with senses so sharp that it could follow every molecule in its course.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this creature from a thought experiment about sorting gas molecules by speed.

tossups.p: In 1912, Marian Smoluchowski [“smoh-loo-KOF-skee”] showed that a spring-loaded trapdoor could not do this being’s job automatically, because random bumps from molecules would make the trapdoor itself jiggle open and shut.
tossups.r: It seems to break the second law of thermodynamics. For 10 points, name this imaginary molecule-sorter from a thought experiment by a Scottish physicist.

tossups.p: Thomas Pynchon’s novel _The Crying of Lot 49_ features the Nefastis Machine, a box that supposedly holds one of these beings. Its inventor claims that a specially gifted person can communicate with the being inside.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this imaginary creature that seems to break the second law of thermodynamics by sorting fast and slow molecules.

tossups.p: In 1951, Léon Brillouin [“bree-YWAN”] argued that this being could not see the molecules it sorts unless it shone light on them, and that the light would add more entropy than its sorting removed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this thought experiment in which a tiny being sorts gas molecules by speed.

tossups.p: Its creator first described this thought experiment in an 1867 letter to his friend Peter Guthrie Tait, and he later included it in his 1871 book _Theory of Heat_.
tossups.r: In it, a tiny being lets only fast molecules through a door one way and slow ones the other way. For 10 points, name this imaginary creature.

tossups.p: This being takes advantage of the fact that molecules in a gas at one temperature move at a wide range of speeds, described by a distribution named for Ludwig Boltzmann and this being’s creator.
tossups.r: By sorting the molecules, it would make one chamber hot and the other cold. For 10 points, name this imaginary creature.

tossups.p: If this being really worked, it would let an engine run forever on the heat of its surroundings, a so-called perpetual motion machine of the second kind. It would not break the first law of thermodynamics, since the total energy of the gas stays the same.
tossups.r: It seems to break the second law instead. For 10 points, name this imaginary creature that sorts fast and slow molecules.

tossups.p: Physicists have explained why this being fails by linking heat to information theory, the field that Claude Shannon founded in 1948. The being has to record which molecules it lets through, and that record cannot grow forever.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this imaginary creature that seems to lower entropy by sorting molecules.

tossups.p: This being would make heat flow from a colder region to a hotter one without any work being done, which the Clausius [“KLOU-zee-us”] statement of a law of thermodynamics says is impossible.
tossups.r: That law says entropy never decreases in an isolated system. For 10 points, name this imaginary creature that guards a door between two boxes of gas.

tossups.p: In his famous lectures, Richard Feynman showed that a tiny ratchet attached to a paddle wheel could not do this being’s job, because the ratchet would be jostled by the same random molecular motion it tried to use.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this imaginary creature that sorts fast and slow molecules to seem to break the second law of thermodynamics.

tossups.p: Its creator compared the law this being seems to break to the fact that once you pour a glass of water into the sea, you can never get the same glass of water back out. He said that law is true only statistically.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this imaginary creature that sorts fast and slow molecules between two chambers.

tossups.p: In the original version of this thought experiment, a vessel full of air is divided into two portions, A and B, by a wall with a small hole in it.
tossups.r: A tiny being opens and closes the hole so that fast molecules gather on one side and slow ones on the other. For 10 points, name this imaginary creature.

tossups.p: A refrigerator can move heat from its cold inside to a warmer kitchen only by using energy, usually electricity, but this imaginary being would seem to do the same job for free. Its creator, a Scottish physicist, is better known for his equations of electricity and magnetism.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this imaginary creature that sorts fast and slow molecules, seeming to break the second law of thermodynamics.

Seems to break the second law of thermodynamics by lowering entropy without doing work
Its sorting would make one chamber hot and the other cold, starting from gas at one temperature
Imagined by a Scottish physicist best known for his equations of electricity and magnetism
First described in an 1867 letter to Peter Guthrie Tait; published in the 1871 book _Theory of Heat_
William Thomson (later Lord Kelvin) gave it its common name in 1874
The catch involves information: the being must gather, record, and eventually erase what it knows about each molecule
Its creator used it to show that the second law is a statistical truth, not an absolute one
Landauer’s principle: erasing one bit of information must give off a little heat
It uses the wide spread of molecular speeds in a gas, described by a distribution named for Ludwig Boltzmann and its creator
If it worked, it could power a perpetual motion machine of the second kind
Leo Szilard (1929) imagined a one-molecule “engine” version and argued that gaining information must create entropy
Charles Bennett (1982): the real cost is erasing the being’s memory, not measuring the molecules
Marian Smoluchowski (1912): a spring-loaded trapdoor fails because random molecular bumps jiggle it open and shut
Léon Brillouin (1951): the being needs light to see molecules, and the light adds more entropy than sorting removes
Thomas Pynchon’s _The Crying of Lot 49_ features the Nefastis Machine, a box said to hold one
Richard Feynman’s ratchet and paddle wheel fails for the same reason: random molecular motion jostles the ratchet
Its creator compared the second law to never getting the same glass of water back out of the sea
The original version divides a vessel of air into two portions, A and B, by a wall with a small hole
Its puzzle was solved by linking heat to information theory, which Claude Shannon founded in 1948
It would move heat from cold to hot with no work, which the Clausius statement of the second law forbids
It would not break the first law of thermodynamics, since the total energy stays the same
Would seem to move heat from cold to hot for free, a job a refrigerator can do only by using energy, usually electricity

trap.title: The being, not the law
trap.body: Tossups on this thought experiment are packed with clues about entropy and the second law of thermodynamics, which are separate answer lines, so blurting the law or the quantity is wrong. Laplace’s demon is a different imaginary being, one that could predict the whole future of the universe. Saying just “demon” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this being,” “this creature,” or “this thought experiment” that sorts fast and slow molecules, say “Maxwell’s demon.” Name the second law only when the question asks for “this law.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Maxwell’s demon (prompt on demon; do not accept “second law of thermodynamics”)

topics.name: Lord Rayleigh
topics.kicker: English physicist · Explained the blue sky and co-discovered argon
topics.briefing: Lord Rayleigh, born John William Strutt, was an English physicist who explained in 1871 why the sky is blue: air molecules scatter short blue waves of sunlight far more than long red ones. Years later, he noticed that a liter of nitrogen taken from the air weighed slightly more than a liter made from chemicals, a clue that led him and William Ramsay to discover argon. He won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physics.
topics.answerHtml: Lord Rayleigh (accept John William Strutt; do not accept “William Ramsay”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This scientist explained how a whisper can travel all the way around the curved wall of the gallery at the base of the dome of St. Paul’s Cathedral in London. He discussed it in his two-volume book _The Theory of Sound_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English physicist who explained why the sky is blue.

tossups.p: In 1892, this scientist wrote to the journal _Nature_ asking for help with a puzzle: nitrogen taken from the air weighed slightly more than the same volume of nitrogen made from ammonia. Solving that puzzle led him and a chemist partner to a new element in 1894.
tossups.r: That element was argon. For 10 points, name this English physicist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physics.

tossups.p: A criterion named for this physicist says two points of light can just be told apart when the center of one point’s blurry image falls on the first dark ring around the other’s. He also predicted rolling surface waves from earthquakes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English physicist who explained the blue color of the sky.

tossups.p: With James Jeans, this physicist names a law for the light given off by hot objects that wrongly predicted endless energy at short wavelengths, a failure later nicknamed the “ultraviolet catastrophe.” Max Planck’s radiation law avoids that problem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English physicist who discovered argon with William Ramsay.

tossups.p: This physicist succeeded James Clerk Maxwell as the Cavendish Professor of Experimental Physics at Cambridge in 1879 and held that post until 1884. While there, he helped set accurate standards for electrical units such as the ohm.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English physicist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize for discovering argon.

tossups.p: In 1890, this scientist spread tiny amounts of olive oil on water to find how thin an oil film could get, giving an early estimate of the size of molecules. He also studied how tiny particles scatter light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English physicist who explained why the sky is blue.

tossups.p: This scientist’s “duplex theory” explains that people tell where a sound comes from by comparing when it reaches each ear and how loud it is in each ear. He proposed it decades after writing a famous two-volume book about sound.
tossups.r: That book was _The Theory of Sound_. For 10 points, name this English physicist who co-discovered argon.

tossups.p: This scientist showed that particles much smaller than a light wave scatter it by an amount that grows as one over the wavelength to the fourth power, so short waves are scattered far more than long ones. That kind of scattering is named for him.
tossups.r: It explains why sunsets look red. For 10 points, name this English physicist who explained why the sky is blue.

tossups.p: This physicist married Evelyn Balfour, the sister of future Prime Minister Arthur Balfour, and he did much of his research in a private laboratory at his family’s estate, Terling Place, in Essex.
tossups.r: He explained why the sky is blue. For 10 points, name this English nobleman and physicist who discovered argon with William Ramsay.

tossups.p: Born in 1842 as the son of a baron, this physicist finished first in Cambridge University’s difficult Mathematical Tripos [“TRY-poss”] exams in 1865, earning the title Senior Wrangler. He inherited his father’s title in 1873.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English physicist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering argon.

tossups.p: This physicist and a Scottish chemist discovered a new gas named from the Greek word for “lazy,” because it would not react with other substances. He won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physics, the same year his partner won the prize in chemistry.
tossups.r: That partner was William Ramsay. For 10 points, name this English physicist who explained why the sky is blue.

tossups.p: In 1891, this scientist sent a letter from Agnes Pockels, who had measured surface tension using a homemade trough in her kitchen, to the journal _Nature_, which published it. He had studied oil films on water himself the year before.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English physicist who discovered argon with William Ramsay.

tossups.p: This physicist served as president of the Royal Society from 1905 to 1908 and as Chancellor of the University of Cambridge from 1908 until his death in 1919.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English physicist who explained why the sky is blue and won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physics.

tossups.p: This scientist predicted in 1885 that earthquakes produce a kind of wave that rolls along the ground’s surface like a wave on the ocean. Those waves, named for him, are slower than P and S waves but often do the most damage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English physicist who explained why the sky is blue.

tossups.p: This physicist began writing a famous book about sound while traveling on the Nile River in Egypt, where he had gone to recover from an illness. The book’s first volume was published in 1877.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English physicist, the author of _The Theory of Sound_, who explained why the sky is blue.

Won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physics; Ramsay won the chemistry prize the same year

Began writing _The Theory of Sound_ while traveling on the Nile in Egypt, recovering from an illness

trap.title: The man, not the scattering
trap.body: Several answer lines carry this man’s name, like Rayleigh scattering, Rayleigh waves, and the Rayleigh criterion, so if a question asks for “this process” or “this type of wave,” his name alone is wrong. His partner William Ramsay shares the discovery of argon, so argon clues alone fit both men, and this page does not accept Ramsay.
trap.fix: Physics clues, like the blue sky, sound, earthquake waves, the Cavendish professorship, and the 1904 physics prize, point to Lord Rayleigh. Chemistry clues, like finding neon, krypton, and xenon or isolating helium on Earth, point to Ramsay.
trap.line: Real answer line: Lord Rayleigh (accept John William Strutt; do not accept “William Ramsay”)

topics.name: Millikan oil drop experiment
topics.kicker: The 1909 measurement of the electron’s charge · Proved charge comes in units
topics.briefing: In 1909, Robert Millikan and his student Harvey Fletcher sprayed a fine mist of oil into a chamber holding two metal plates at the University of Chicago. By adjusting the voltage on the plates until a charged droplet hung still in midair, they could work out the electric charge it carried. Every charge they measured was a whole-number multiple of one tiny amount, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs: the charge of a single electron.
topics.answerHtml: Millikan oil drop experiment (accept oil drop experiment; prompt on Millikan; do not accept “cathode ray tube” or “J. J. Thomson”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Felix Ehrenhaft [“AIR-en-hahft”] of Vienna disputed this experiment’s results, claiming to find “subelectrons” with even smaller charges. Decades later, historians studying the lab notebooks of this experiment’s leader found that he had left out many measurements from his famous 1913 paper.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment that measured the charge of the electron using tiny charged droplets.

tossups.p: In a 1974 speech, Richard Feynman described how later measurements of the value found in this experiment crept upward only slowly, because scientists hesitated to report numbers far from it. Its value came out slightly low because it used a wrong value for the viscosity of air.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1909 experiment that measured the electron’s charge by suspending charged droplets between two metal plates.

tossups.p: To find the weight of each droplet in this experiment, its scientists timed how fast the droplet fell with the voltage on the plates switched off and then used Stokes’ law to work out its size from that speed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment that showed electric charge comes in whole-number multiples of the electron’s charge.

tossups.p: Before this experiment, J. J. Thomson, John Townsend, and H. A. Wilson had estimated the electron’s charge by timing how fast whole clouds of tiny water droplets fell, but those droplets evaporated too quickly.
tossups.r: This experiment instead watched single droplets one at a time. For 10 points, name this 1909 experiment that measured the charge of the electron.

tossups.p: Harvey Fletcher worked on this experiment as a graduate student, but the key 1910 paper on its results listed only his professor as the author. Fletcher’s own account of their work was published in 1982, after his death.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment, performed at the University of Chicago, that measured the charge of a single electron.

tossups.p: When X-rays struck the air inside this experiment’s chamber, a droplet could gain or lose charge, and its speed then changed by a whole step, never by part of a step.
tossups.r: That showed that charge is quantized. For 10 points, name this experiment whose result, about 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs, is the charge of one electron.

tossups.p: Inside this experiment’s apparatus, an atomizer sprayed a fine mist, and a few droplets drifted down through a tiny hole into the space below. A bright light made the droplets look like tiny stars against a dark background.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment that balanced charged droplets in an electric field to find the charge of the electron.

tossups.p: Combining this experiment’s result with J. J. Thomson’s charge-to-mass ratio let scientists calculate the mass of the electron. Combining it with the Faraday constant gave a much better value of Avogadro’s number.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1909 experiment that measured the elementary charge using tiny charged droplets between two plates.

tossups.p: The scientist who led this experiment won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics, partly for this work and partly for testing Albert Einstein’s equation for the photoelectric effect. He later wrote that confirming Einstein’s equation went against all his own expectations.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment that measured the charge of the electron by balancing tiny charged droplets.

tossups.p: Physicists have run automated versions of this experiment on huge numbers of droplets, searching for free particles with one-third of the usual charge, such as lone quarks, without finding any. Quarks carry one-third or two-thirds of the electron’s charge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1909 experiment that first precisely measured the charge of a single electron.

tossups.p: The leader of this experiment later headed the California Institute of Technology and popularized the name “cosmic rays” for high-energy radiation from space. He moved there from the University of Chicago in 1921.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment that measured the charge of the electron by watching tiny charged droplets.

tossups.p: This experiment’s 1913 paper reported that every charge it measured was a whole-number multiple of one basic unit, named in the paper’s title as the “elementary electrical charge.”
tossups.r: That unit is the charge of one electron. For 10 points, name this experiment that balanced tiny charged droplets between two metal plates.

tossups.p: In its full form, this experiment timed each droplet twice: falling under gravity with the field off, and rising with the field switched on and pulling it upward.
tossups.r: In the simpler textbook version, a droplet hangs still when the electric force balances its weight. For 10 points, name this experiment that measured the electron’s charge.

tossups.p: Each droplet in this experiment quickly stopped speeding up as it fell, once the push of the air balanced its weight, so its scientists could time its steady speed with a stopwatch. That steady speed is called terminal velocity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment that showed electric charge comes in units of about 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs.

tossups.p: This experiment’s leader first tried water, but the tiny water droplets evaporated too quickly to be timed for long, so the team switched to a liquid that evaporates very slowly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment that measured the charge of the electron, performed at the University of Chicago in 1909.
