Performed starting in 1909 at the University of Chicago, with the help of graduate student Harvey Fletcher
Balanced tiny charged droplets between two metal plates by adjusting the voltage (the electric field)
Showed that charge comes only in whole-number multiples of one basic unit: charge is quantized
A droplet hangs still when the upward electric force equals its weight (charge = weight ÷ field)
An atomizer sprayed a fine mist; a few droplets drifted through a tiny hole into the space below
X-rays changed a droplet’s charge, and its speed changed by whole steps, never by part of a step
Each falling droplet quickly reached a steady speed (terminal velocity), timed with a stopwatch
Stokes’ law turned a droplet’s steady falling speed into its size and weight
Its leader won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics, partly for it and partly for testing Einstein’s photoelectric equation
With J. J. Thomson’s charge-to-mass ratio (1897), its result gave the electron’s mass
With the Faraday constant, its result gave a much better value of Avogadro’s number
Water droplets evaporated too fast, so the team switched to a slowly evaporating liquid
Earlier, Thomson, John Townsend, and H. A. Wilson timed whole falling clouds of water droplets
Felix Ehrenhaft of Vienna disputed it, claiming to find smaller “subelectrons”
Historians studying its leader’s notebooks found he left many measurements out of his 1913 paper
Richard Feynman’s 1974 “cargo cult science” speech told how later values crept up only slowly from its result
Its value came out slightly low because it used a wrong value for the viscosity of air
Fletcher’s own account was published in 1982, after his death; the key 1910 paper listed only his professor
Lit by a bright lamp, the droplets looked like tiny stars against a dark background
Its full method timed each droplet falling with the field off and rising with the field on
Automated versions have searched huge numbers of droplets for one-third charges, like lone quarks, without finding any
Its leader later headed Caltech and popularized the name “cosmic rays”
Its 1913 paper’s title calls the basic unit the “elementary electrical charge”

trap.title: The experiment, not the particle
trap.body: Tossups on this experiment are full of clues about electrons and electric charge, which are separate answer lines. J. J. Thomson’s cathode ray tube is a different famous experiment: it discovered the electron in 1897, while this one measured the electron’s charge. The Michelson–Morley experiment is another famous American experiment whose name starts with “Mi-.”
trap.fix: Droplets, an atomizer, two charged plates, hovering, and 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs point to this experiment. A glowing beam bent by magnets and the charge-to-mass ratio point to Thomson; light beams and the aether point to Michelson–Morley. Saying just “Millikan” earns a prompt, so add “oil drop experiment.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Millikan oil drop experiment (accept oil drop experiment; prompt on Millikan; do not accept “cathode ray tube” or “J. J. Thomson”)

topics.name: Magnetic monopoles
topics.kicker: Hypothetical lone magnetic poles · Never found, but physics allows them
topics.dates: Predicted by Paul Dirac, 1931; never confirmed
topics.briefing: Cut a bar magnet in half and you never get a lone north pole and a lone south pole: you get two smaller magnets, each with both. A magnetic monopole would be a particle with just one magnetic pole, the way an electron carries just one kind of electric charge. In 1931, Paul Dirac showed that even one monopole anywhere in the universe would explain why electric charge comes in fixed amounts, but no one has ever confirmed finding one.
topics.answerHtml: magnetic monopoles (accept monopoles; prompt on magnetic charge; do not accept “magnetic dipole”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On February 14, 1982, Blas Cabrera’s superconducting loop at Stanford recorded a single jump in current that looked like one of these particles passing through. The event was never repeated, so physicists do not count it as a discovery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles that would carry a single north or south magnetic pole.

tossups.p: In 1931, Paul Dirac showed that if even one of these particles exists anywhere in the universe, then electric charge must come in whole-number multiples of a smallest unit. That would explain why all electric charges in nature come in fixed amounts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles, never confirmed, that would be lone north or south magnetic poles.

tossups.p: Gauss’s law for magnetism, one of Maxwell’s equations, says that the total magnetic flux out of any closed surface is zero, which means these objects do not appear in classical physics. If one were found, that equation would have to change.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles that would have only a north pole or only a south pole.

tossups.p: Alan Guth’s theory of cosmic inflation was proposed partly to explain why the universe is not full of these heavy particles, which grand unified theories predict should have formed in huge numbers just after the Big Bang.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these never-confirmed particles, each of which would have a single magnetic pole.

tossups.p: In 1932, Carl Anderson discovered the positron, the antimatter twin of the electron. Paul Dirac had predicted that particle a year earlier, in the same paper in which he argued that these particles could exist.
tossups.r: No one has ever confirmed finding one of these. For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles that would act as isolated north or south magnetic poles.

tossups.p: The MoEDAL experiment at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider was built mainly to search for these particles in the debris of proton collisions. Part of the experiment is designed to trap any that are made, so they can be studied later.
tossups.r: None has ever been confirmed. For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles with only one magnetic pole.

tossups.p: In materials called spin ice, defects in the arrangement of tiny atomic magnets behave like imitation versions of these particles. Physicists stress that these “quasiparticles” are not true elementary examples.
tossups.r: Paul Dirac argued that they could exist. For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles that would have only one magnetic pole, unlike every magnet ever found.

tossups.p: If these objects existed, the equations of electricity and magnetism would become almost perfectly symmetrical, with a magnetic version of electric charge. A single electron is the electric counterpart of one of these objects.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles that would be lone north or south magnetic poles.

tossups.p: A loop of superconducting wire can serve as a detector for these particles, because one passing through the loop would cause a sudden, lasting jump in the current flowing around it.
tossups.r: Each one would be a lone north or south pole. For 10 points, name these never-confirmed particles that would carry magnetic charge.

tossups.p: In 1894, Pierre Curie, who later shared a Nobel Prize with his wife, Marie, suggested that free magnetic charges might exist in nature. His paper discussed the possible existence of “free magnetism.” Decades later, Paul Dirac gave the first strong argument from quantum theory that they could exist.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles that would each have just a north or just a south pole.

tossups.p: Unlike electric field lines, which begin on positive charges and end on negative charges, magnetic field lines always form closed loops, because no one has ever confirmed finding one of these objects.
tossups.r: Paul Dirac predicted them in 1931. For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles that would be isolated north or south magnetic poles.

tossups.p: The IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole has searched for fast-moving examples of these particles by looking for the light they would give off as they sped through the ice.
tossups.r: Cutting a bar magnet in half never produces one of these. For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles with a single magnetic pole.

tossups.p: Physicists searched moon rocks brought back by Apollo astronauts for trapped examples of these particles, without success. In that search, the samples were passed through a superconducting coil to look for a sudden, lasting jump in current.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles, each a lone north or south magnetic pole.

tossups.p: Because of a property called spin, a single electron acts like a tiny bar magnet with both a north and a south pole. That is one reason why breaking a magnet into smaller and smaller pieces never produces one of these objects.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles that would be single north or south magnetic poles.

tossups.p: Italy’s MACRO experiment, buried deep under a mountain, took its name partly from these particles, which it searched for during the 1990s without finding any. The experiment also studied cosmic rays and neutrinos.
tossups.r: Every magnet ever found has two poles. For 10 points, name these hypothetical particles that would carry a lone north or south magnetic pole.

clues.t: Hypothetical particles with just one magnetic pole: a lone north or a lone south
Cutting a bar magnet in half never makes one; each half gets its own north and south poles
Never confirmed in any experiment, as of 2025
Each would carry “magnetic charge,” a magnetic version of electric charge
Paul Dirac (1931): if even one exists, electric charge must come in fixed units (charge quantization)
Magnetic field lines always form closed loops, since no lone poles have been found
Gauss’s law for magnetism, one of Maxwell’s equations, says the total magnetic flux out of any closed surface is zero
If they existed, the equations of electricity and magnetism would be almost perfectly symmetrical
A single electron is the electric counterpart; a magnet with two poles is a dipole
Blas Cabrera’s superconducting loop at Stanford recorded one possible event on February 14, 1982, never repeated
One passing through a superconducting loop would cause a sudden, lasting jump in current
Alan Guth’s cosmic inflation was proposed partly to explain why the universe isn’t full of them
Grand unified theories predict extremely heavy ones that formed just after the Big Bang
Dirac’s 1931 paper on them also predicted the antielectron (positron), which Carl Anderson discovered in 1932
The MoEDAL experiment at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider was built mainly to search for them
In spin ice, defects among tiny atomic magnets imitate them, but these quasiparticles are not true elementary ones
Pierre Curie suggested in 1894 that free magnetic charges might exist
The IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole has searched for light from fast-moving ones
Apollo moon rocks were passed through a superconducting coil to search for trapped ones, without success
Because of its spin, even a single electron acts like a tiny bar magnet with both poles, so breaking magnets never makes one
Italy’s MACRO experiment, deep under a mountain, searched for them in the 1990s and found none

trap.title: One pole, not two
trap.body: Every magnet ever found is a dipole, with both a north and a south pole, so “magnetic dipole” is the opposite of this answer. Tossups about these particles also mention magnetic fields, Gauss’s law for magnetism, and Paul Dirac, which are separate answer lines. Saying “magnetic charge” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Lone north or south poles, Dirac’s 1931 argument, Cabrera’s 1982 event, and the cosmic inflation puzzle point to these particles. If the question asks for “this law” or “this equation,” the answer is Gauss’s law for magnetism instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: magnetic monopoles (accept monopoles; prompt on magnetic charge; do not accept “magnetic dipole”)

topics.name: Density
topics.kicker: Mass packed into a given space · Why ice floats and rocks sink
topics.dates: Archimedes’ crown test, 3rd century BCE (traditional story)
topics.briefing: Density tells you how much mass is packed into a given space: a brick and a block of foam the same size have very different densities. You find it by dividing an object’s mass by its volume, and anything less dense than water, like a block of wood, floats on it. Water itself is a strange case: it is densest at about 4 °C, and ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice cubes float.
topics.answerHtml: density (accept mass density; prompt on specific gravity, relative density, or rho; do not accept “mass” or “volume”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Henry Cavendish’s 1798 experiment, often described as “weighing the world,” found Earth’s average value of this quantity to be about five and a half times that of water. Earth has the highest value of this quantity of any planet in the solar system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, found by dividing an object’s mass by its volume.

tossups.p: A Galileo thermometer works because its glass bulbs rise or sink as this property of the liquid around them changes with temperature. Each bulb carries a small tag marked with a temperature.
tossups.r: Of the planets, only Saturn has a lower average value of this property than water. For 10 points, name this property, measured in grams per cubic centimeter.

tossups.p: Osmium has the highest value of this property of any element, just ahead of iridium, while lithium has the lowest value of any metal and can even float on water. A block of osmium has about twice the mass of a lead block the same size.
tossups.r: Objects with more of it than water sink. For 10 points, name this property, equal to mass per unit volume.

tossups.p: According to a story told by the Roman writer Vitruvius [“vih-TROO-vee-us”], Archimedes [“ar-kih-MEE-deez”] figured out how to test whether King Hiero’s [“HY-er-ohz”] crown was pure gold while stepping into a bath, then ran home shouting “Eureka!”
tossups.r: He realized that the water pushed aside would reveal the crown’s volume. For 10 points, name this property, mass divided by volume, that showed whether the crown was pure gold.

tossups.p: Lakes freeze from the top down partly because liquid water reaches its greatest value of this property at about 4 °C, so the water at the bottom of a deep lake stays near that temperature all winter.
tossups.r: Ice floats because it has less of this property than liquid water. For 10 points, name this property, an object’s mass divided by its volume.

tossups.p: Submarines dive and surface by flooding or emptying ballast tanks, which changes their overall value of this quantity compared with the seawater around them. Many fish do the same job by adjusting the gas in a swim bladder.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity whose value for pure water is 1 gram per cubic centimeter.

tossups.p: A hydrometer floats higher in liquids that have more of this property, so the mark on its stem at the surface tells the value. Dividing this property of a substance by that of water gives a unitless number called specific gravity.
tossups.r: Things with less of it than water float. For 10 points, name this property calculated as mass divided by volume.

tossups.p: An iron or lead cannonball floats on liquid mercury, because mercury has a greater value of this property than either metal. Gold, however, sinks in mercury. Mercury has about 13.5 times as much of this property as water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, symbolized by the Greek letter rho, which equals mass divided by volume.

tossups.p: Very salty water has more of this property than fresh water, which is why swimmers float so easily in the Dead Sea and why a raw egg that sinks in tap water can float in strong salt water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, which tells whether an object will sink or float in a liquid.

tossups.p: In the North Atlantic, cold, salty seawater sinks because it has a high value of this quantity, helping drive a slow, worldwide loop of deep ocean currents called the thermohaline circulation. Antarctic Bottom Water has the highest value of this quantity of any large mass of ocean water.
tossups.r: Warm air rises for the opposite reason. For 10 points, name this quantity, mass per unit volume.

tossups.p: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball about the size of a city, giving it an enormous value of this quantity. A white dwarf has a smaller but still huge value of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity found by dividing an object’s mass by its volume.

tossups.p: A can of regular soda usually sinks in a tank of water while a can of diet soda floats, because the sugar dissolved in regular soda raises this property.
tossups.r: A classroom “tower” stacks honey, water, and oil in layers by this property. For 10 points, name this property, mass divided by volume.

tossups.p: Water has roughly 800 times as much of this quantity as air at sea level. At a fixed pressure, heating a gas lowers this quantity, which is why a hot-air balloon rises through the cooler air around it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, an object’s mass per unit volume, often given in grams per cubic centimeter.

tossups.p: Hydrogen bonds lock frozen water molecules into an open, six-sided pattern with lots of empty space, so water expands by about nine percent when it freezes and its value of this property drops.
tossups.r: That is why ice floats. For 10 points, name this property, an object’s mass divided by its volume.

tossups.p: The kilogram was first based on the mass of one liter of water, so water’s value of this quantity was set at one kilogram per liter. Seawater has slightly more of this quantity than fresh water.
tossups.r: To find this quantity for a rock, measure its volume by how much water it pushes aside, then divide its mass by that volume. For 10 points, name this quantity.

clues.t: Equals mass divided by volume (ρ = m/V)
Often measured in grams per cubic centimeter; pure water has 1 g/cm³
Objects with less of it than water float; objects with more sink
Ice has less of it than liquid water, so ice floats
Symbolized by the Greek letter rho (ρ)
Liquid water has the most of it at about 4 °C, so the bottom of a deep lake stays near 4 °C in winter
In the traditional story, Archimedes used it to test King Hiero’s gold crown, then ran from the bath shouting “Eureka!”
Find an irregular object’s volume by the water it pushes aside in a graduated cylinder
Saturn is the only planet with less of it than water; Earth has the most of any planet
Osmium has the highest value of any element, just ahead of iridium
Specific gravity compares it with water’s value, giving a unitless number
A hydrometer floats higher in liquids with more of it
Heating a gas lowers it, so hot-air balloons rise
Salt water has more of it than fresh water, so people float easily in the Dead Sea
Henry Cavendish (1798), “weighing the world,” found Earth’s average value is about 5.5 times water’s
Lithium has the lowest value of any metal and can float on water
Iron and lead cannonballs float on liquid mercury (about 13.5 times water’s value), but gold sinks in it
A Galileo thermometer’s tagged glass bulbs rise or sink as the liquid’s value changes with temperature
Submarines flood or empty ballast tanks, and fish adjust swim bladders, to change their overall value
Cold, salty water sinks in the North Atlantic, helping drive the thermohaline circulation
A neutron star squeezes more mass than the Sun into a ball about the size of a city
Regular soda cans usually sink in water while diet soda cans float, because of dissolved sugar
Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open, six-sided pattern, so water expands about 9% when it freezes
The kilogram was first based on the mass of one liter of water
The crown story was told by the Roman writer Vitruvius
Water has roughly 800 times as much of it as air at sea level
A block of osmium has about twice the mass of a lead block the same size

trap.title: Not mass, not volume
trap.body: This quantity is built from two others, mass and volume, and tossups mention both, so players blurt one of them. Mass is how much matter an object has and volume is how much space it takes up; this answer is the ratio between them. Buoyancy, the upward push of a fluid, shows up in the same questions but is a separate answer, and “specific gravity” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Mass divided by volume, grams per cubic centimeter, rho, floating and sinking, and ice floating point to this answer. If the question asks for “this upward force,” say buoyancy instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: density (accept mass density; prompt on specific gravity, relative density, or rho; do not accept “mass” or “volume”)

topics.name: Drag (physics)
topics.kicker: The force that resists motion through air or water · Why parachutes work
topics.briefing: Drag is the force that pushes back on anything moving through air or water, from a cyclist to a swimmer to a jumbo jet. It grows quickly with speed, which is why a falling skydiver eventually stops speeding up at a steady terminal velocity, and why a parachute, with its huge area, slows the fall to a gentle landing. Engineers fight drag by giving cars, planes, and racing bikes smooth, streamlined shapes.
topics.answerHtml: drag (accept drag force, air resistance, or fluid resistance; prompt on friction; do not accept “lift”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Golf balls have dimples because the dimples help the air flowing past cling to the ball longer, shrinking the low-pressure wake behind it and so reducing this force. Swimmers shave and wear slick suits to reduce this force in water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this force that resists the motion of an object through a fluid such as air or water.

tossups.p: Stokes’ law says that for a tiny sphere moving slowly through a fluid, this force equals six pi times the fluid’s viscosity times the sphere’s radius and speed. Robert Millikan used that law to find the sizes of his charged droplets.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this force that opposes motion through a fluid and makes falling objects reach terminal velocity.

tossups.p: Car designers test models in wind tunnels to lower this force’s namesake coefficient. At highway speeds, this force roughly quadruples whenever a car’s speed doubles, so on the highway it uses up much of a car’s fuel.
tossups.r: Parachutes use it to slow a fall. For 10 points, name this force that streamlined shapes are designed to reduce.

tossups.p: A skydiver who tucks into a head-down dive can fall much faster than one falling belly-down, because the smaller area facing the air cuts this force. Belly-down skydivers stop speeding up at roughly 200 kilometers per hour.
tossups.r: When this force balances a falling object’s weight, the object reaches terminal velocity. For 10 points, name this force.

tossups.p: Isaac Newton studied this force in Book II of his _Principia_, arguing that for many objects moving through air or water it grows roughly with the square of their speed. He measured it by watching how quickly swinging pendulums slowed down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this force that acts on a moving object opposite to its motion through a fluid.

tossups.p: Racing cyclists ride in tight lines so that riders behind can tuck into the leader’s wake, where this force is much weaker, a trick called drafting. Race car drivers use the same trick at high speed.
tossups.r: Streamlined shapes reduce it. For 10 points, name this force that resists objects moving through air.

tossups.p: In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the Moon, and they hit the ground together, because the Moon has almost no air to cause this force.
tossups.r: On Earth, this force makes a feather fall slowly. For 10 points, name this force that resists motion through air.

tossups.p: Spinning maple seeds and fluffy dandelion seeds take advantage of this force to fall slowly, so the wind can carry them far from the parent plant. A flat sheet of paper falls slowly, but the same sheet crumpled into a ball falls fast, because crumpling reduces this force.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this force that a parachute uses to slow a falling skydiver.

tossups.p: Thin traces of air in low Earth orbit slowly pull the International Space Station lower through this force, so it has to be boosted back up from time to time by rocket thrusters.
tossups.r: Returning spacecraft use this force to slow down in the atmosphere. For 10 points, name this force that resists motion through air.

tossups.p: The Reynolds number compares a fluid’s inertia to its viscosity. At low Reynolds numbers, such as for a bacterium swimming, this force grows in direct proportion to speed, but for a fast-moving car it grows with the square of speed.
tossups.r: Teardrop-shaped, streamlined bodies reduce this force. For 10 points, name this force that resists motion through a fluid.

tossups.p: Downhill skiers crouch into a tight “tuck” position and speed skaters wear smooth, hooded suits to reduce this force, which grows quickly as they go faster. Cyclists in time trials wear pointed, teardrop-shaped helmets for the same reason.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this force that a streamlined shape helps reduce, which acts opposite to an object’s motion through air.

tossups.p: Europe’s Huygens [“HOY-gunz”] probe floated down through the thick, hazy air of Saturn’s moon Titan for more than two hours in 2005, slowed by parachutes that relied on this force.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this force, which grows with an object’s speed and with the area it presents to the air.

tossups.p: Airplane wings produce an “induced” type of this force as a side effect of making lift, and many airliners have upturned winglets at their wingtips to reduce it. That type is strongest when a plane flies slowly, as during takeoff and landing.
tossups.r: Of the four forces on a flying airplane, this one opposes thrust. For 10 points, name this force.

tossups.p: Gustave Eiffel studied this force by dropping objects from his famous tower in Paris, and he later built wind tunnels to measure it on models of airplane wings. He published his results in the early 1900s.
tossups.r: Parachutes increase it. For 10 points, name this force that resists the motion of a falling object through the air.

tossups.p: A diving peregrine falcon pulls its wings tight against its body to cut this force, letting it reach speeds of more than 300 kilometers per hour. Tuna and dolphins have torpedo-shaped bodies to reduce this force as they swim.
tossups.r: It grows as an object moves faster through air or water. For 10 points, name this force that parachutes are designed to increase.

clues.t: A force that resists an object’s motion through a fluid, such as air or water
When it balances a falling object’s weight, the object stops speeding up: terminal velocity
Parachutes use their large area to increase it and slow a fall
Streamlined, teardrop shapes, as on cars, planes, and fish, reduce it
One of the four forces on a flying airplane; it opposes thrust, while lift opposes weight
At highway speeds it roughly quadruples when speed doubles (it grows with the square of speed)
Engineers calculate it with a namesake equation that uses its coefficient, measured in wind tunnels
It depends on the fluid, the object’s speed, its shape, and the area facing the flow
On the Moon in 1971, Apollo 15’s David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather that fell together, since there is almost no air
Drafting: cyclists and race cars ride in a leader’s wake, where it is weaker
A belly-down skydiver stops speeding up at roughly 200 km/h; a head-down dive cuts it and falls faster
Sometimes called fluid friction, but a separate answer from sliding friction between solid surfaces
Golf ball dimples shrink the low-pressure wake behind the ball, reducing it
Stokes’ law: for a tiny, slow sphere it equals 6π × viscosity × radius × speed (used by Millikan)
The Reynolds number compares inertia to viscosity; at low values it grows in proportion to speed, at high values with speed squared
Isaac Newton studied it in Book II of his _Principia_, watching how swinging pendulums slowed
Spinning maple seeds and fluffy dandelion seeds use it to fall slowly and drift far
Thin air in low orbit slowly pulls the International Space Station lower, so it must be boosted back up
The Huygens probe’s parachutes relied on it to slow the probe through Titan’s thick air for more than two hours in 2005
Wings make an “induced” type as a side effect of lift; winglets reduce it, and it is strongest at low speeds
Gustave Eiffel dropped objects from his tower and built wind tunnels to measure it
Downhill skiers tuck, speed skaters wear smooth suits, and cyclists wear teardrop helmets to reduce it
A diving peregrine falcon pulls in its wings to cut it, passing 300 km/h
Swimmers shave and wear slick suits to reduce it in water; tuna and dolphins are torpedo-shaped
Flat paper falls slowly but crumpled paper falls fast, because crumpling reduces it

trap.title: Not lift, not just friction
trap.body: This force is sometimes called “fluid friction,” but quiz bowl treats it as a separate answer from friction between two solid surfaces, so saying just “friction” earns only a prompt. On airplanes it is one of four forces, so players blurt “lift,” which pushes a plane up, or “thrust,” which pushes it forward. And “terminal velocity” is a speed, not a force.
trap.fix: Air or water, parachutes, streamlining, wind tunnels, and speed squared point to this force; sliding surfaces, lubricants, and the coefficient mu times the normal force point to friction. On an airplane, the force that opposes thrust is this one, while lift opposes weight.
trap.line: Real answer line: drag (accept drag force, air resistance, or fluid resistance; prompt on friction; do not accept “lift”)

topics.name: Semiconductors
topics.kicker: Materials between conductors and insulators · The heart of computer chips
topics.dates: First transistor built at Bell Labs, 1947
topics.briefing: Semiconductors are materials, like silicon and germanium, that conduct electricity better than insulators such as rubber but worse than metals such as copper. Adding a pinch of another element, called doping, lets engineers control exactly how well they conduct. That trick made possible the transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, and billions of tiny silicon transistors fill the chips inside phones and computers.
topics.answerHtml: semiconductors (accept semiconducting materials; prompt on metalloids; do not accept “superconductors” or “insulators”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1833, Michael Faraday noticed that silver sulfide conducted electricity better as it got hotter, the opposite of how metals behave, an early example of these materials. In 1874, Karl Ferdinand Braun [“BROWN”] found that a metal point touching certain crystals of these materials let current pass more easily one way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these materials, such as silicon and germanium, whose ability to conduct falls between that of metals and insulators.

tossups.p: The Czochralski [“choh-KRAHL-skee”] process grows huge single crystals of one of these materials by slowly pulling a seed crystal upward out of a pool of the melted material. The crystals are then sliced into thin wafers for making chips.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these materials, such as silicon, that conduct electricity better than insulators but worse than metals.

tossups.p: In these materials, the band gap, the energy an electron needs to jump from the valence band into the conduction band, is small enough that some electrons make the jump at room temperature.
tossups.r: Insulators have much larger band gaps. For 10 points, name these materials, such as silicon, that conduct better than insulators but not as well as metals.

tossups.p: Adding a little phosphorus or arsenic, whose atoms have five valence electrons, to one of these materials leaves extra free electrons and makes it “n-type.” Each added atom has one more valence electron than the atoms it replaces.
tossups.r: Adding boron instead creates positive “holes” and makes it p-type. For 10 points, name these materials whose conductivity can be controlled by doping.

tossups.p: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for research on these materials and for the discovery of the transistor effect. Shockley later invented an improved “junction” version of their device.
tossups.r: Their first transistor was built at Bell Labs in 1947. For 10 points, name these materials, such as silicon and germanium.

tossups.p: The first transistor, built in December 1947, used a slab of one of these materials touched by two gold contacts placed very close together. Walter Brattain and John Bardeen built it at Bell Labs in New Jersey.
tossups.r: That material was germanium. For 10 points, name these materials whose conductivity is between that of conductors and insulators.

tossups.p: John Bardeen, a co-inventor of a device made from these materials, later won a second Nobel Prize in Physics for explaining superconductivity, making him the only person to win that prize twice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these materials, such as silicon, used to build transistors and computer chips, whose conductivity can be changed by doping.

tossups.p: Unlike metals, these materials usually conduct electricity better when they are heated, which lets some of them serve as temperature sensors called thermistors. Heat gives more electrons enough energy to jump across the material’s band gap.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these materials, like silicon and germanium, whose conductivity lies between that of metals and insulators.

tossups.p: In 1956, William Shockley set up a laboratory in California to make devices from these materials, but in 1957 eight of his employees, later nicknamed the “traitorous eight,” left to found the company Fairchild.
tossups.r: California’s Silicon Valley is named for one of these materials. For 10 points, name these materials used to make computer chips.

tossups.p: Jack Kilby built the first integrated circuit in 1958, and Robert Noyce soon built a more practical one, each putting several parts of a circuit onto a single chip of one of these materials. Kilby won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics for that work.
tossups.r: Kilby used germanium and Noyce used silicon. For 10 points, name these materials whose conductivity is between that of conductors and insulators.

tossups.p: In a light-emitting diode made of these materials, the color of the light depends on the size of the band gap, so blue light needs a material with a wide gap, such as gallium nitride.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these materials, like silicon, used to make diodes, transistors, and solar cells.

tossups.p: Dmitri Mendeleev [“men-duh-LAY-ef”] predicted one element used in these materials in 1871, calling it “eka-silicon,” and Clemens Winkler discovered it in 1886, naming it for his home country. Mendeleev’s predictions of its properties turned out to be remarkably close.
tossups.r: That element is germanium. For 10 points, name these materials, such as germanium and silicon, that conduct better than insulators but worse than metals.

tossups.p: Measuring the Hall effect in one of these materials reveals whether its current is carried mainly by negative electrons or by positive “holes.” That effect is much stronger in these materials than in metals, which have far more free electrons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these materials that can be made n-type or p-type by adding tiny amounts of other elements.

tossups.p: Many spacecraft solar panels use gallium arsenide, one of these materials, because it turns sunlight into electricity more efficiently than ordinary solar cells do. In a typical solar cell, light striking the boundary between two specially treated layers knocks electrons loose and drives them around a circuit.
tossups.r: Those layers are p-type and n-type versions of these materials. For 10 points, name these materials, such as silicon and germanium.

tossups.p: In a crystal of a typical one of these materials, each atom shares electrons with four neighbors in covalent bonds, and a missing electron, called a hole, can move through the crystal like a positive charge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these materials, used in computer chips, that conduct better than insulators but not as well as metals.

clues.t: Conduct electricity better than insulators but worse than metals
The best-known examples are silicon and germanium, metalloids in group 14
Used to make transistors, diodes, solar cells, and computer chips
The transistor was invented from them at Bell Labs in 1947
Doping: adding tiny amounts of other elements controls how well they conduct

p-type: doped with boron or gallium (three valence electrons), creating positive “holes”
Have a small band gap between the valence band and the conduction band; insulators have a large one
Usually conduct better when heated, the opposite of metals
Joining p-type and n-type layers makes a p-n junction, the heart of diodes, LEDs, and solar cells
John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics
California’s Silicon Valley is named for the silicon in computer chips
Michael Faraday (1833) saw silver sulfide conduct better when hotter, an early example
Karl Ferdinand Braun (1874): a metal point touching certain crystals let current pass more easily one way
The Czochralski process pulls a big single crystal from a melt using a seed crystal; it is sliced into wafers
The first transistor (December 1947) used germanium touched by two gold contacts
John Bardeen later won a second physics Nobel (1972) for explaining superconductivity
In 1957, the “traitorous eight” left Shockley’s California lab to found Fairchild
Jack Kilby (1958, germanium) and Robert Noyce (silicon) built the first integrated circuits; Kilby won the 2000 Nobel Prize
An LED’s color depends on its band gap; blue LEDs need a wide-gap material like gallium nitride
Mendeleev predicted germanium as “eka-silicon” (1871); Clemens Winkler found it in 1886 and named it for Germany
The Hall effect shows whether current is carried by electrons or holes, and it is much stronger in them than in metals
Gallium arsenide solar cells power many spacecraft because they are very efficient
Each atom in a silicon crystal shares electrons with four neighbors; a missing electron (a hole) moves like a positive charge
Thermistors use them as temperature sensors because their conductivity changes with heat

trap.title: Semi-, not super-
trap.body: Semiconductors and superconductors sound alike but behave very differently: a superconductor has zero resistance when it is very cold, while these materials conduct only partly and usually conduct better when warmed. Insulators, like rubber and glass, barely conduct at all. Players also blurt devices made from these materials, like transistors or diodes, or a single element like silicon.
trap.fix: Silicon and germanium, doping, n-type and p-type, holes, band gaps, and Bell Labs point to these materials. Zero resistance, the Meissner effect, and extreme cold point to superconductors; if the question asks for “this device,” name the transistor or diode instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: semiconductors (accept semiconducting materials; prompt on metalloids; do not accept “superconductors” or “insulators”)
